I'd like some tips for setting up a NAS

• Personally, I would go for the Red. Green ones are known to fail fairly fast (~1 year) in 24/7 configurations.
  • Not really my area of expertise I'll admit, you'd have to consult some build-a-pc lads.
  • No experience with BTRFS, so no opinion from me on that.
  • Maybe something like OpenMediaVault or NAS4Free, which is a fork of the old FreeNAS code.

• What kind of drives to use depends on how you're going to use them. If you're using a RAID controller, then you should avoid "green" drives. If you're doing software RAID, then the drives won't matter as much. ZFS for example isn't going to mark a drive as bad just because it had a bit of extra latency on a write or whatever. I run "green" drives with ZFS and haven't had any issues. You should also take a look at Toshiba and HGST, as they're both pretty consistent at making reliable drives for a reasonable price.

  • An inexpensive dual core will be more than sufficient. The case really depends. I'm partial to Fractal Design. Their Node series cases might fit the bill depending on how many drives are you planning on using. As for energy efficiency, use a PSU calculator and choose your power supply wisely. You probably won't need a high wattage model, and running a high wattage PSU at low load is something to avoid.

  • If data integrity is your chief concern, then ZFS is the way to go and I'd urge you to take another look at it. Damn near every UNIX-like operating system supports it, and it's one of the most advanced file systems available to you right now. You'll have some learning to do in order to implement it properly, but it's worth a little of your time. You'll also save on a potentially expensive RAID controller. Most systems have more than enough CPU power to spare for calculating parity, and file systems like ZFS do a far better job of protecting your data.

  • BTRFS isn't done yet, but from what I've read, it does work. The more mature option is ZFS, which is more popular than you might think. You'll have to do some reading and decide which is right for you, but if it isn't critical stuff then there's no reason to rule out BTRFS. Just remember to keep a backup of anything you don't want to lose, no matter what you do otherwise.

  • Use whatever OS you like. I like NAS4Free where the system's only job is to be a NAS. I run Fedora on my own system, because it has many roles. You'll obviously have the easiest time with whatever you're most comfortable with. If you aren't very experienced yet, there's really no harm in running NAS4Free or FreeNAS from a USB stick as a temporary solution. ZFS pools migrate from one OS to another easily.

If you want to learn about ZFS, this is a great resource: https://pthree.org/2012/04/17/install-zfs-on-debian-gnulinux/
